# A Life Worth Sharing

[Silas Bambil · November 2024]{.meta}

For years, whenever I thought about the future, I thought largely about what I wanted to accomplish. I had a fairly clear idea of the education I wanted, the career I hoped to pursue, and the standard of living I wanted to attain. I had given considerably less thought to the person with whom I might eventually share all these things. Marriage was something I expected to consider when other aspects of my life were sufficiently settled. In November 2024, however, companionship began to occupy a different place in my understanding of the future.

I enjoy my independence, and I do not consider my life incomplete because I am unmarried. I take pleasure in pursuing my interests, making my own decisions, and working towards the things I want for myself. Yet I have come to recognise how much enjoyment companionship might add to a life I already find meaningful. A good meal is enjoyable whether one eats alone or in the company of another person. Still, there are people whose presence can make an otherwise unremarkable meal the most enjoyable part of one's day. That possibility appeals to me.

One of the beautiful things about being loved is knowing that you occupy a place in someone's thoughts even when you are nowhere near them. Something amusing happens during their day, and they make a mental note to tell you about it later. They remember something you mentioned weeks ago and ask how it eventually turned out. Among the countless things competing for their attention, they still find themselves thinking about you. To everyone else, these details may be insignificant, but affection makes the ordinary details of another person's life interesting.

Equally appealing is the pleasure of being known. At work, we demonstrate what we are capable of doing. In academic settings, we demonstrate what we know. Even socially, we sometimes make an effort to appear more interesting or composed than we actually are. It would be wonderful to have someone who gradually becomes familiar with the person behind all these efforts, someone who knows my peculiar habits and understands that there will be days when I have very little to say or nothing particularly impressive to offer.

Allowing someone to know you that well requires trust. Some aspects of ourselves are easy to share because we are proud of them; others are more difficult to reveal. I would like to experience the freedom of admitting uncertainty, acknowledging a mistake, or discussing something that troubles me without feeling that I have diminished myself in another person's eyes. More importantly, I want my wife to experience that same freedom around me. She should never feel obliged to present a carefully edited version of herself to deserve my affection.

Then there is the pleasure of loving someone. I imagine how wonderful it must be to look forward to hearing her voice, to remember something she mentioned in passing, or to find myself smiling at the thought of something she said earlier. Her excitement about an upcoming event might become my excitement too, even when the event has little to do with me. There is genuine satisfaction in making someone happy simply because her happiness matters to you. Love offers the unusual privilege of having reasons to be happy that originate in someone else's life.

I genuinely want to like the woman I marry. Beyond being attracted to her and loving her, I want to enjoy her personality. I would love for us to have conversations that begin with something serious and somehow end with both of us laughing about something entirely unrelated. I look forward to hearing her thoughts and discovering the little peculiarities that might make me smile. She need not understand my enthusiasm for everything I enjoy, nor must I share every interest of hers. How wonderful it would be to marry someone whose company I would have sought even if romance had never entered the picture.

A marriage will contain relatively few wedding anniversaries compared with the number of ordinary Tuesdays two people will spend together. There will be meals to prepare, errands to run, work to finish, and evenings when neither person has anything particularly interesting to report. Yet these are among the things I find myself looking forward to. Years later, some of our fondest memories may turn out to be occasions on which we had made no particular effort to create a memory. A conversation over dinner or an evening spent laughing about something ridiculous may outlive the memory of a carefully planned celebration.

One thing I would particularly like is to marry someone who has been genuinely loved at home. Our families often provide our earliest impressions of what it means to care about another person. Through the relationships we observe and experience while growing up, we begin to understand how affection is expressed, how disagreements are handled, and what it means to be treated with kindness. I find the prospect of sharing my life with someone who has experienced that kind of affection appealing. There is value in learning early in life that being loved need not involve constantly earning someone's approval.

However, people arrive at an understanding of love in different ways. Some learn to give affection because they received it generously; others learn because they understand what its absence feels like. A difficult childhood does not prevent someone from becoming a wonderful partner, just as a loving upbringing does not guarantee that someone will become one. We can reflect on what we experienced growing up and decide what we wish to carry into our own homes. Ultimately, what matters to me is how someone has learnt to love and how she chooses to treat the people she loves.

Compatibility matters to me because affection alone cannot settle every question that arises when two people decide to build a life together. Decisions about family, finances, careers, and where to live may reveal differences that were previously of little consequence. What I find reassuring is the prospect of discussing such matters with someone without either of us feeling that our concerns are being dismissed. Being understood can sometimes be just as comforting as having someone agree with us. How we treat each other when we disagree may ultimately reveal more about our compatibility than the number of things on which we agree.

I have little interest in marrying someone who thinks exactly as I do. Part of the pleasure of knowing another person lies in discovering perspectives that would never have occurred to you on your own. I remain ambitious, and I hope she will have ambitions of her own. Whatever form they take, I would enjoy hearing her speak enthusiastically about them and celebrating achievements that have absolutely nothing to do with me. There should be aspects of her life that are distinctly hers. Loving her does not require me to be involved in everything from which she derives happiness.

Another fascinating aspect of marriage is that the person one marries will continue to change. The woman I marry may develop new interests, reconsider ambitions she once held, or discover things about herself that neither of us could have anticipated. I will undoubtedly change in some respects too. In a sense, two people who marry are making a commitment to versions of each other that do not yet exist. Even after years of marriage, I would like to remain curious about her. Knowing someone for a long time should never become a reason to assume that there is nothing more to discover.

I would still like to secure a good, stable job before getting married. Financial security matters to me because I want to be in a reasonable position to contribute to the practical needs of a family. I do not expect to become wealthy before marriage, nor do I believe there is a particular amount of money that makes someone ready for it. Financial difficulties can place genuine pressure on a relationship, and I would prefer to prepare for the obligations I can reasonably anticipate rather than assume that affection will somehow make them disappear.

Nevertheless, even a good job cannot tell me what my financial circumstances will look like ten years from now. Preparing for marriage should not become an indefinite wait for a degree of certainty that life rarely offers. Besides, I could spend years preparing myself financially and still give insufficient attention to becoming someone who is pleasant to live with. A stable income may contribute to a stable household, but it does not automatically create a loving home. The ability to provide for someone deserves attention, as does the ability to make that person feel loved.

Sometimes I consider what it would mean for a woman to choose me as her husband. She will have had a life of her own before meeting me, with people she loves, ambitions she wants to pursue, and ideas about what she wants her future to look like. That she might eventually decide to share a substantial part of that future with me is something I would never want to take for granted. I hope that, many years into our marriage, she will still find reasons to be pleased about having made that decision.

It is easy to imagine oneself being patient when there is nothing to be frustrated about, affectionate when one is well rested, and understanding when another person's needs do not interfere with one's own. Practising these things when they are inconvenient requires more than good intentions. I would like my wife to feel comfortable telling me when I have upset her, knowing that she does not first have to establish that her feelings are justified. The qualities I hope to find in a partner are also qualities against which I must examine my own behaviour.

Loving someone, however, should offer more pleasure than simply knowing that one has fulfilled a responsibility. I imagine the satisfaction of making her day a little easier because I genuinely want to, remembering something she likes, or recognising when she needs a little time to herself. What makes her feel loved may not always be what would make me feel loved. Learning these things about her would be part of the pleasure of knowing her. I hope familiarity never makes me less inclined to express the affection that brought us together in the first place.

There is an obvious advantage to imagining the person one hopes to marry: she exists almost entirely within one's preferences. She has none of the habits that might eventually prove irritating and none of the opinions that might challenge one's expectations. A real person will be far more interesting than that. She will have her own history, peculiarities, preferences, and ways of understanding the world. Some of the things I eventually love most about her may be things I have never thought to look for. I hope I leave enough room in my expectations to discover them.

Love is a good thing. I appreciate it more now than I did when marriage was simply something I expected to consider at some distant point in my life. I know there will be disagreements, difficult decisions, and days when neither of us is particularly easy to be around. Still, I look forward to loving someone whose arrival I am happy about and whose absence I notice. For years, much of my attention had been directed towards becoming the person I wanted to be and building the life I wanted to live. I now find myself giving just as much thought to becoming someone with whom another person would want to share hers. And I look forward to the day when some of the happiest things I have to tell will begin with the word *we*.

Love,

SB
